blocks.text: Practice long questions for the whole of Chapter 18 (Quantum Physics), in the shape of a Board long question: each theory question of 5 marks (define, explain, derive) is followed by a numerical of 3 marks on the same topic. Each question has a model answer; the numericals are solved step by step.

blocks.prompt: 1 State Planck's quantum theory of radiation. What is a photon? Derive expressions for the energy and momentum of a photon, and explain why quantum effects are noticed only for atom sized objects. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Quantum theory (Planck, 1901): Energy is radiated or absorbed in discrete packets of energy called quanta rather than as a continuous wave. Each quantum is associated with radiation of a single frequency f, and its energy is proportional to f:
E = hf ... (18.1)
where h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s is Planck's constant.

Photon: Planck assumed that the granular nature of radiation from hot bodies was due to some property of the atoms producing it. Einstein extended the idea: tiny bundles of energy are an integral part of all electromagnetic radiation and cannot be sub-divided. These indivisible bundles are called photons. A beam of light of wavelength λ is a stream of photons travelling at speed c, each of energy E = hf = hc/λ.

Momentum of a photon: From the theory of relativity E = mc², and the relativistic momentum of the photon is p = mc. Hence
E = pc ... (18.2)
Thus pc = hf, or p = hf/c. Since c = fλ,
p = h/λ ... (18.3)

Why quantum effects appear only for atom sized objects: Quantum theory can be extended to any system, such as a mass oscillating on a spring, but there the energy steps are far too small to be detected, so any particle nature is invisible. Quantum effects are important only for atom sized objects, where h is a significant factor in any detectable energy change.

book_ref.quote: Einstein extended his idea and postulated that packets or tiny bundles of energy are integral part of all electromagnetic radiations

blocks.prompt: 2 Orange light has wavelength 600 nm. Find (i) the energy of one photon in joule and in eV (ii) the momentum of the photon. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Use E = hc/λ for the energy, divide by 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ for eV, and p = h/λ for the momentum.

book_ref.quote: The energy E of each quantum is proportional to its frequency f related as

blocks.prompt: 3 Describe the apparatus used to study the photoelectric effect. Explain how the stopping potential gives the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons, how the photocurrent depends on intensity and frequency, and why these results cannot be explained by the wave theory of light. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Photoelectric effect: The emission of electrons from a metal surface when exposed to light of suitable frequency or wavelength. The emitted electrons are photoelectrons.

Apparatus (Fig. 18.1): An evacuated glass tube contains two electrodes. The anode A is connected to the positive terminal of the battery and the metal cathode C to the negative terminal. When monochromatic light of suitable frequency falls on C, it emits electrons, which are attracted by the positive anode; the current is measured by a micro-ammeter. The current stops when light is cut off, so it flows because of the incident light: photoelectric current.

Stopping potential: Reverse the battery so that A is negative and C positive. The photoelectrons are repelled and the current decreases. When the anode is made more and more negative, at a certain value V₀, the stopping potential, the current becomes zero: even the electrons of maximum energy cannot reach the anode. So
½mv²max = V₀e ... (18.4)

Effect of intensity (Fig. 18.2): With higher intensity (I₂ > I₁) the current increases, but it stops at the same V₀.
Effect of frequency (Fig. 18.3): At constant intensity the current is the same, but V₀ is different for each frequency, so (K.E.)max increases with frequency.

Results:
(i) Electrons are emitted with different energies; the maximum energy depends on the metal surface and the frequency of light.
(ii) There is a threshold frequency f₀ below which no electrons are emitted, however intense the light (blue light ejects electrons from sodium, red light does not). f₀ varies from metal to metal; the corresponding wavelength is the threshold wavelength.
(iii) Electrons are emitted instantaneously; the intensity determines only their number.

Failure of wave theory: According to the electromagnetic wave theory, higher intensity should increase the K.E. of the electrons, which contradicts experiment. It also cannot explain the threshold frequency: even light of lesser energy should eventually transfer enough energy to liberate electrons, but this does not happen.

book_ref.quote: The photoelectric effect is demonstrated by the apparatus shown in Fig. 18.1.

blocks.prompt: 4 In a photoelectric experiment the stopping potential is 0.80 V when photons of energy 2.8 eV fall on the cathode. Find (i) the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons in joule (ii) their maximum speed (m = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg) (iii) the work function of the cathode in eV. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: The stopping potential gives (K.E.)max = V₀e; from ½mv²max get vmax; the photon energy minus (K.E.)max is φ.

book_ref.quote: where m is mass, v is velocity and e is the charge on electron.

blocks.prompt: 5 Explain the photoelectric effect on the basis of quantum theory. Derive Einstein's photoelectric equation and write it in terms of the threshold frequency. Why does the equation hold only for some of the emitted electrons? (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Quantum explanation: Einstein extended Planck's idea: light is emitted or absorbed in quanta called photons, each of energy E = hf. A photon is absorbed by a single electron in the metal surface. The electron needs a certain minimum energy, the work function φ, to escape. If the photon energy is sufficient, the electron is ejected instantaneously: part of the photon energy breaks it away from the metal and the rest appears as its kinetic energy.

Derivation:
Incident photon energy − Work function = (K.E.)max of photoelectron
hf − φ = ½mv²max ... (18.5)
This is Einstein's photoelectric equation.

Threshold frequency: When (K.E.)max = 0, f equals the threshold frequency f₀, so
hf₀ − φ = 0, or φ = hf₀ ... (18.6)
Substituting in Eq. 18.5:
(K.E.)max = hf − hf₀ ... (18.7)
So for f < f₀ no electrons are emitted, and (K.E.)max increases with f, not with intensity; more intense light means more photons, hence more electrons.

Why only some electrons: All emitted electrons do not have the maximum kinetic energy; some come straight out of the surface and some lose energy in atomic collisions before coming out. Eq. 18.7 holds only for electrons that come out with the full surplus energy.

The effect cannot be explained if light is a wave with energy uniformly spread over its wavefront; it shows the particle nature of light. Einstein received the 1921 Nobel Prize for this explanation.

book_ref.quote: A photon could be absorbed by a single electron in the metal surface.

blocks.prompt: 6 The work function of a metal is 2.2 eV. Light of wavelength 420 nm falls on it. Find (i) the threshold frequency (ii) the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons in eV (iii) the stopping potential. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Get f₀ from φ = hf₀, the photon energy from hc/λ, then (K.E.)max = hf − φ and V₀ = (K.E.)max/e.

book_ref.quote: Hence, we can also write Einstein's photoelectric equation as

blocks.prompt: 7 What is the Compton effect? Using conservation of energy and momentum, write the equations for the collision of an X-ray photon with an electron at rest, state the expression for the Compton shift, and explain the Compton wavelength. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Compton effect: Compton (1923) scattered X-rays from loosely bound electrons of a graphite target (Fig. 18.5) and found that the wavelength of the scattered X-rays is larger than that of the incident X-rays. Classical wave theory could not explain this. Compton treated X-rays as photons of energy hc/λ and momentum h/λ.

Collision (Fig. 18.6): An X-ray photon of energy hf = hc/λ strikes an electron at rest, like a billiard ball. The photon is scattered at angle θ with a smaller energy hf′ = hc/λ′, and the electron recoils at angle φ with K.E. = (m − m₀)c², where m is its mass when moving with velocity v and m₀ its rest mass. It is an elastic collision: energy and momentum are both conserved.

Conservation of energy:
Change in photon energy = K.E. of electron
hf − hf′ = mc² − m₀c²
hc/λ − hc/λ′ = (m − m₀)c²

Conservation of momentum (a vector, so along x and y):
x-component (original direction): h/λ + 0 = (h/λ′) cos θ + mv cos φ
y-component: 0 + 0 = (h/λ′) sin θ − mv sin φ

Result: Solving these equations gives
λ′ = λ + (h/m₀c)(1 − cos θ)
Δλ = λ′ − λ = (h/m₀c)(1 − cos θ) ... (18.8)

Compton wavelength: h/m₀c has dimensions of wavelength:
h/m₀c = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴)/(9.1 × 10⁻³¹ × 3 × 10⁸) = 2.43 × 10⁻¹² m
At θ = 90°, Δλ equals the Compton wavelength. Eq. 18.8 agreed completely with Compton's results, a striking confirmation of the particle like interaction of electromagnetic waves with matter.

book_ref.quote: Consider scattering of a photon by an electron in which the photon suffers collision with the electron like a billiard ball.

blocks.prompt: 8 X-rays of wavelength 20.0 pm are scattered through 120° by loosely bound electrons. Find (i) the Compton shift (ii) the wavelength of the scattered X-rays (iii) the energies of the incident and scattered photons in keV. (h/m₀c = 2.43 pm) (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Put θ = 120° in Δλ = (h/m₀c)(1 − cos θ), add it to λ, then use E = hc/λ for each photon.

book_ref.quote: If the scattered X-ray photons are observed at θ = 90°, the Compton shift Δλ equals the Compton wavelength.

steps: E′ = hc/λ′ = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3 × 10⁸)/(23.65 × 10⁻¹²) = 8.41 × 10⁻¹⁵ J = 52.6 keV (the electron takes the difference, 9.6 keV)
blocks.final_answer: (i) Δλ = 3.65 pm (ii) λ′ ≈ 23.6 pm (iii) E = 62.2 keV, E′ = 52.6 keV

blocks.prompt: 9 Describe the interaction of electromagnetic radiation with matter at low, intermediate and high photon energies. Explain pair production with its energy equation, find the minimum photon energy needed for it, and explain annihilation of matter. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Interaction with matter:
(i) At low energies (less than 0.5 MeV) the dominant process is the photoelectric effect: the photon is absorbed by an electron, which is ejected.
(ii) At intermediate energies the dominant process is the Compton effect: the photon is scattered by an electron with a longer wavelength.
(iii) At higher energies (more than 1.2 MeV) the dominant process is pair production.

Pair production: A very high energy photon, such as a γ-ray, interacting with matter is changed into an electron-positron pair, according to Einstein's energy equation:
Energy of photon = Energy needed for pair production + K.E. of the particles
hf = 2m₀c² + K.E.(e⁻) + K.E.(e⁺) ... (18.9)
where m₀c² is the rest mass energy of the electron (and of the positron).

Minimum energy: The least photon energy is when both particles have zero K.E.:
hf(min) = 2m₀c² = 2 × 0.51 MeV = 1.02 MeV
(0.51 MeV is the rest mass energy of an electron, as used in Example 18.3.) A photon with more energy gives the extra energy to the pair as K.E.

Annihilation of matter: The converse of pair production. A particle and its antiparticle interact and annihilate into high energy photons in the γ-ray range:
e⁻ + e⁺ = γ + γ
For an electron-positron pair at rest, each of the two photons carries 0.51 MeV, of wavelength λ = hc/E = 2.43 pm (Example 18.3).

book_ref.quote: It is pair production in which photon energy is changed into electron-positron pair

blocks.prompt: 10 A γ-ray photon of energy 2.50 MeV produces an electron-positron pair. The rest mass energy of an electron is 0.51 MeV. Find (i) the total kinetic energy of the pair (ii) the kinetic energy of each if shared equally (iii) the minimum frequency of a photon that can produce a pair. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Use hf = 2m₀c² + K.E.(e⁻) + K.E.(e⁺); the minimum photon energy is 2m₀c², then f = E/h.

book_ref.quote: the converse of pair-production is known as annihilation of matter

blocks.prompt: 11 State de Broglie's hypothesis and derive the de Broglie relation. Using the examples of a rifle bullet and an electron, explain why wave effects are observed for electrons but not for objects of everyday life. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Hypothesis: Light displays a dual nature: it acts as a wave and as a particle. Assuming symmetry in nature, Louis de Broglie proposed in 1924 that material particles should also possess wave-like properties.

Derivation: The momentum of a photon is
p = h/λ (Eq. 18.3)
de Broglie suggested that the momentum of a material particle of mass m moving with velocity v is given by the same expression:
p = h/λ = mv
λ = h/p = h/mv ... (18.10)
where λ is the wavelength of the particle waves. This is the de Broglie relation; an electron can therefore be considered both a particle and a wave.

Rifle bullet (m = 20 g, v = 330 m s⁻¹):
λ = h/mv = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴/(2 × 10⁻² × 330) = 1 × 10⁻³⁴ m
This is so small that it cannot be measured or detected by any of its effects. An object of large mass and ordinary speed has negligible interference and diffraction effects.

Electron (v = 1 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹):
λ = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴/(9.1 × 10⁻³¹ × 1 × 10⁶) = 7 × 10⁻¹⁰ m
This is in the X-ray range, so diffraction effects for electrons are measurable, whereas interference effects for bullets are not.

de Broglie received the 1929 Nobel Prize for his work on the dual nature of particles.

book_ref.quote: It has been observed that light displays a dual nature, it acts as a wave and it acts as a particle.

blocks.prompt: 12 Find the de Broglie wavelength of (i) a proton (m = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg) moving at 2.0 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹ (ii) a cricket ball of mass 0.05 kg moving at 20 m s⁻¹. Which one can show diffraction? (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Apply λ = h/mv to each, then compare the wavelengths with atomic sizes.

book_ref.quote: where λ is the wavelength associated with particle waves.

steps: The proton's wavelength is small but measurable (diffraction of protons has been observed); the ball's is far too small to detect.
blocks.final_answer: (i) λ(proton) = 1.99 × 10⁻¹² m (ii) λ(ball) = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ m; only the proton can show diffraction

blocks.prompt: 13 Describe the Davisson and Germer experiment. Derive the de Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated through a potential difference V, and show how the experiment confirmed the de Broglie wavelength. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Experiment (Fig. 18.7): Electrons from a heated filament are accelerated by an adjustable voltage V in an electron gun. The beam, of energy Ve, is made incident on a nickel crystal. The beam diffracted from the crystal surface enters a detector and is recorded as a current I. The scattered electrons came off in regular peaks, interpreted as diffraction, just like X-ray diffraction by an NaCl crystal. So electrons are diffracted from metal crystals exactly like X-rays.

Derivation: The gain in K.E. of the electron accelerated through V is
½mv² = Ve
mv² = 2Ve, or m²v² = 2mVe
mv = √(2mVe)
From de Broglie's equation λ = h/mv:
λ = h/√(2mVe) ... (18.11)

Confirmation: In one experiment V = 54 V:
λ = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴/√(2 × 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ × 54 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹) ≈ 1.67 × 10⁻¹⁰ m (the book gives 1.66 × 10⁻¹⁰ m)
The diffracted beam was obtained at a glancing angle of 65°. By Bragg's equation 2d sin θ = mλ, with m = 1 and d = 0.91 × 10⁻¹⁰ m for nickel:
λ = 2 × 0.91 × 10⁻¹⁰ × sin 65° = 1.65 × 10⁻¹⁰ m
The experimental wavelength agrees excellently with the predicted one.

Diffraction has also been observed with protons, neutrons, hydrogen and helium atoms, giving substantial evidence for the wave nature of particles. Davisson and G. P. Thomson shared the 1937 Nobel Prize.

book_ref.quote: A convincing evidence of the wave nature of electrons was provided by Clinton J. Davisson

blocks.prompt: 14 Electrons are accelerated from rest through 150 V and diffracted by a nickel crystal (d = 0.91 × 10⁻¹⁰ m). Find (i) the momentum of the electrons (ii) their de Broglie wavelength (iii) the glancing angle for first order diffraction. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Find mv = √(2mVe), then λ = h/mv, then Bragg's equation 2d sin θ = λ for m = 1.

book_ref.quote: This beam of electrons diffracted from crystal surface was obtained for a glancing angle of 65°.

blocks.prompt: 15 What is wave-particle duality? Using experiments on light and on electrons, explain Bohr's principle of complementarity and how the nature of an experiment decides which aspect is revealed. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Evidence for light: Interference and diffraction of light show its wave nature; the photoelectric effect and Compton effect prove its particle nature.
Evidence for electrons: The experiments of Davisson and Germer and of G. P. Thomson reveal the wave-like nature of electrons, while in J. J. Thomson's e/m experiment the particle-like nature of the electron had to be assumed. A beam of electrons through a double slit gives bright and dark fringes, as light does, not just two images of the slits.

Wave-particle duality: We must assume both wave-like and particle-like properties for all matter (electrons, protons, neutrons, molecules) and for radiation (light, X-rays, γ-rays). Matter and radiation have a dual 'wave-particle' nature; this is wave-particle duality. All micro-particles propagate as if they were waves and exchange energies as if they were particles.

Principle of complementarity (Niels Bohr): Both wave and particle aspects are required for a complete description of radiation and matter. Both are always present and either may be revealed by an experiment, but both cannot be revealed simultaneously in a single experiment.

Role of the experiment: The two aspects are different 'faces' that light shows to experimenters; the nature of the experiment decides which is seen. A diffraction grating in the path of a light beam reveals it as a wave; light hitting a metal surface must be regarded as a stream of particles. No simple experiment requires us to treat the beam as a wave and a particle at the same time. Light behaves as a stream of photons when it interacts with matter and as a wave while travelling from source to detector.

book_ref.quote: Niels Bohr pointed out in stating his principle of complementarity

blocks.prompt: 16 A photon and an electron (m = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg) each have a wavelength of 0.20 nm. Find (i) the energy of the photon in eV (ii) the speed of the electron (iii) the kinetic energy of the electron in eV. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: For the photon E = hc/λ; for the electron the same wavelength gives momentum h/λ = mv, so v and ½mv² follow.

book_ref.quote: In effect, all micro-particles (electrons, protons, photons, atoms, etc.)

steps: Electron: mv = h/λ = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴/(0.20 × 10⁻⁹) = 3.32 × 10⁻²⁴ kg m s⁻¹
blocks.final_answer: (i) 6.2 × 10³ eV (6.2 keV) (ii) 3.64 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ (iii) 37.7 eV: same wavelength, very different energies

blocks.prompt: 17 Explain the principle and working of the transmission electron microscope with a labelled description of its lenses. Why is its resolution much higher than that of an optical microscope? Give its uses. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Principle: The electron microscope uses the wave nature of electrons. Their de Broglie wavelength is about a thousand times shorter than the wavelength of visible light, so it can see fine details not visible to an optical microscope.

Working (Fig. 18.8):
(i) Electrons from a source are accelerated by applying voltages of several megavolts.
(ii) They pass through an electromagnetic lens called the condenser, which focuses the beam on the specimen.
(iii) An electromagnetic objective lens forms the image of the specimen.
(iv) The image is further magnified by the electromagnetic projector lens to photograph it on a film, called a micrograph.

Resolution: λ = h/mv. The higher the speed of the electrons, the shorter the wavelength and hence the higher the resolution. So the electron microscope can see much smaller details, down to the nano-metric, i.e. about the atomic, level. Modern scanning electron microscopes give three dimensional images of remarkable quality.

Uses: study of cell structure, viruses and bacteria in microbiology; investigation of metal fractures; study of materials and crystal structure.

book_ref.quote: The electrons from a source are passed through the electromagnetic lens called condenser

blocks.prompt: 18 In an electron microscope, electrons are accelerated from rest through 5.0 kV. Find (i) their momentum (ii) their de Broglie wavelength (iii) how many times shorter it is than light of wavelength 550 nm. (Treat the electrons non-relativistically.) (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Use mv = √(2mVe) and λ = h/mv, then divide 550 nm by λ.

book_ref.quote: The higher is the speed of electrons, the shorter is the wavelength and hence, higher is the resolution.

blocks.final_answer: (i) 3.82 × 10⁻²³ kg m s⁻¹ (ii) λ = 1.74 × 10⁻¹¹ m (iii) about 3.2 × 10⁴ times shorter

blocks.prompt: 19 Describe the experimental arrangement for observing atomic spectra. Write the formulas for the Balmer, Lyman and Paschen series of hydrogen with their regions and the values of n, and explain how the emission spectrum arises from ground and excited states. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Arrangement (Fig. 18.9): A discharge tube, a spectrometer and a diffraction grating. A series of lines is seen on a dark background through the eyepiece. The vapours of different elements show different patterns of lines, called spectral series, which identify the elements.

Balmer series (visible): Identified by J. J. Balmer (1885) in the spectrum of atomic hydrogen; it consists of four lines in the visible region. Rydberg's formula:
1/λ = R_H(1/2² − 1/n²), n = 3, 4, 5, ...
where R_H = 1.0974 × 10⁷ m⁻¹ is the Rydberg constant.

Lyman series (ultraviolet):
1/λ = R_H(1/1² − 1/n²), n = 2, 3, 4, ... (18.12)

Paschen series (infrared):
1/λ = R_H(1/3² − 1/n²), n = 4, 5, 6, ... (18.13)

Energy levels and emission (Figs. 18.11, 18.12): These equations give the allowed energy values of the electron in isolated hydrogen atoms. The state n = 1 is the ground state; n = 2, 3, 4, ... are excited states. An atom absorbs energy only in discrete amounts and is raised to an excited state. Excited states have very short life; the electron soon returns to a lower level by emitting photons, observed as the emission spectrum of several spectral lines. Transitions ending on n = 1 give the Lyman series, on n = 2 the Balmer series and on n = 3 the Paschen series.

book_ref.quote: The evidence of particle nature of quantized photons using spectrometer is the basis of atomic spectra.

blocks.prompt: 20 Find (i) the wavelength of the second line of the Balmer series (n = 4 to n = 2) (ii) the energy of its photon in eV. (R_H = 1.0974 × 10⁷ m⁻¹) (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Put n = 4 in the Balmer formula to get 1/λ, invert, then E = hc/λ.

book_ref.quote: where n is the discrete excited energy level of the electrons with values 3,4,5,... and R_H is the Rydberg constant.

blocks.prompt: 21 Explain how an atom is excited by absorbing energy and how it returns. Using this, explain why the dark lines in the absorption spectrum of an element appear at the same wavelengths as the bright lines of its emission spectrum. State the condition for excitation by a photon and by an electron, and name the types of spectra. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Excitation and return: An atom absorbs energy only in discrete amounts and its electron makes a transition to a higher energy level (excited state). Excited states have very short life; the electron returns to a lower level by emitting a photon. The photon's energy equals the energy difference of the two levels:
hf = Eₙ − Eₚ

Absorption spectrum: When light with a continuous spectrum, such as white light, passes through a gas at low pressure, light of certain wavelengths is missing and dark lines are seen in their places. As the light passes through, electrons absorb discrete amounts of energy for upward transitions; only photons of certain energy or frequency are absorbed, exactly matching the energy needed.

Emission spectrum: When these excited electrons return to lower levels, photons of the same specific wavelengths are emitted, giving the emission line spectrum.

Relation (Fig. 18.13): The same pairs of levels are involved in both, so the wavelengths missing from the absorption line spectrum are exactly those present in the emission line spectrum of the same element.

Condition for excitation: A photon must have energy exactly equal to the energy difference between the two levels, but an electron with K.E. greater than or equal to the difference can excite the gas atoms.

Types of spectra: continuous spectrum, line spectrum and band spectrum.

book_ref.quote: As the light passes through the gas, electrons absorb discrete amount of energy and make transition to higher energy levels.

blocks.prompt: 22 A hydrogen atom in the ground state absorbs a photon and is raised to the level n = 3. Using 1/λ = R_H(1/1² − 1/n²), find (i) the wavelength of the photon absorbed (ii) the energy difference between the two levels in eV (iii) the least kinetic energy of an electron that could cause the same excitation. (R_H = 1.0974 × 10⁷ m⁻¹) (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: The absorbed wavelength is the Lyman line for n = 3; its photon energy hc/λ is the level difference; an electron needs at least that much K.E.

book_ref.quote: The wavelengths of light absorbed correspond exactly to energy needed to make such upward transitions.

steps: An electron needs K.E. greater than or equal to the difference: K.E.(min) = 12.1 eV

blocks.prompt: 23 State Heisenberg's uncertainty principle and derive Δx.Δp ≈ h using a photon of wavelength λ. Use it to show that electrons cannot exist inside the nucleus, and write the energy-time form and Heisenberg's more careful forms of the principle. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Statement: Position and momentum of a particle cannot be measured simultaneously with perfect accuracy. This fundamental uncertainty is not due to the measuring instrument; it is a consequence of the wave-particle duality of matter and radiation (Heisenberg, 1927). It is negligible for macroscopic objects (photons hardly affect a flying tennis ball) but predominant in the atomic domain (one photon drastically alters an electron's motion).

Derivation: Light has wave properties, so the position of an electron can be found only to within one wavelength of the light used. If light of wavelength λ locates a micro-particle moving along the x-axis:
Δx ≈ λ
At most the photon can transfer all its momentum h/λ to the particle, so
Δp ≈ h/λ
Multiplying:
Δx.Δp ≈ λ(h/λ) ≈ h ... (18.14)
The product of the uncertainty Δx in position and the uncertainty Δp in the x-component of momentum at the same instant approximately equals h. Light of shorter wavelength reduces Δx but alters the motion drastically, making Δp larger.

Electrons not in the nucleus: A nucleus is of the order of 10⁻¹⁵ m, so Δx ≈ 10⁻¹⁵ m:
Δp ≈ h/Δx ≈ 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴/1 × 10⁻¹⁵ ≈ 6.63 × 10⁻¹⁹ kg m s⁻¹
The corresponding energy uncertainty is of the order of GeV. No such electron is found in the atom, so electrons do not exist inside the nucleus.

Energy-time form:
ΔE.Δt ≈ h ... (18.15)
The more accurately the energy of a particle is determined, the more uncertain the time during which it has that energy.

Heisenberg's careful forms: At the very best
Δx.Δp ≥ ħ and ΔE.Δt ≥ ħ, where ħ = h/2π = 1.05 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.

book_ref.quote: If light of wavelength λ is used to locate a micro-particle moving along x-axis, the uncertainty in its position measurement is:

blocks.prompt: 24 Answer both parts: (i) An electron (m = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg) is confined to a region 5.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ m wide. Find the uncertainty in its momentum and velocity. (ii) An excited atom radiates for about 2 × 10⁻⁹ s. Find the uncertainty in the energy of the emitted photon in eV. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Use Δp ≈ h/Δx and Δv = Δp/m for (i), and ΔE ≈ h/Δt for (ii).

book_ref.quote: Using the formula Δp.Δx ≈ h As Δp ≈ mΔv Hence mΔv.Δx = h, Δv = h/(m × Δx)

blocks.final_answer: (i) Δp = 1.33 × 10⁻²⁴ kg m s⁻¹, Δv = 1.46 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ (ii) ΔE = 2.1 × 10⁻⁶ eV
